Yes, though I walk through the valley of the Shadow.
—Psalm of David.

You who read this are still among the living. But I who write it will long since have passed into the region of shadows. Strange things will happen, secrets will become known, and many centuries will pass before people see this record. When they do, some will disbelieve it, some will doubt it, and a few will find much to consider in these letters engraved with an iron stylus.

It had been a year of terror, and of feelings more intense than terror, for which there is no name on earth. Many strange wonders and signs had appeared, and the black wings of Pestilence spread far and wide over sea and land. Those skilled in reading the stars knew that the heavens showed an evil aspect. To me, the Greek Oinos, among others, it was clear that the change of that seven hundred and ninety-fourth year had now arrived, when, at the entrance to Aries, Jupiter joins the red ring of terrible Saturnus. Unless I am greatly mistaken, the strange spirit of the skies showed itself not only in the physical earth, but in human souls, imaginations and thoughts.

At night, in a dim city called Ptolemais, seven of us sat with flasks of red Chian wine inside a grand hall. Our room had only one entrance: a tall brass door made by the craftsman Corinnos. It was a work of rare skill, and it was locked from within. Black hangings in the gloomy room hid the moon, the lurid stars and the empty streets from our view. But they could not shut out the foreboding and memory of Evil. There were things around us that I cannot clearly describe, both physical and spiritual: heaviness in the air, a sense of suffocation, anxiety, and above all that terrible state familiar to the nervous, when the senses are intensely alive and awake but the power of thought lies asleep. A dead weight hung over us. It hung upon our limbs, upon the furniture, upon the goblets we drank from. Everything was pressed down and burdened by it—everything except the flames of the seven lamps lighting our revelry. They rose in tall, slender lines of light and burned pale and motionless. Their light made a mirror of the round ebony table where we sat. In it, each of us saw the pallor of his own face and the restless glare in his companions’ lowered eyes. Yet we laughed and made merry in our own way, which was hysterical. We sang the songs of Anacreon, which are madness, and drank deeply, although the purple wine reminded us of blood. For there was another occupant of our room: young Zoilus. He lay dead, stretched out in his shroud, the presiding spirit and demon of the scene. Alas, he took no part in our merriment, except that his face, distorted by plague, and his eyes, in which Death had only half extinguished the disease’s fire, seemed to take whatever interest the dead may take in the merriment of those who will die. Although I, Oinos, felt the dead man’s eyes upon me, I forced myself not to notice the bitterness of their expression. Staring steadily into the depths of the ebony mirror, I sang the songs of the son of Teios in a loud, ringing voice. Gradually my songs stopped. Their echoes rolled away among the room’s black hangings, grew faint and indistinct, and faded. Then, from those black hangings where the sounds had died, a dark, undefined shadow emerged. It was like a shadow the low moon might cast from a human figure, but it belonged neither to a person nor to a God, nor to anything familiar. For a while it trembled among the hangings. At last it settled in full view on the brass door. But the shadow was vague, shapeless and indistinct. It was the shadow neither of a person nor of a God—neither a God of Greece, nor a God of Chaldaea, nor any Egyptian God. It rested on the brass doorway beneath the arch of the door’s ornamental upper structure. It did not move or speak. It became still there and remained. If I remember correctly, the door on which the shadow rested was opposite the feet of the shrouded young Zoilus. We seven had seen the shadow come from the hangings, but did not dare look steadily at it. We lowered our eyes and kept gazing into the depths of the ebony mirror. At last I, Oinos, spoke a few quiet words and asked the shadow its name and where it lived. The shadow answered, “I am SHADOW. My home is near the Catacombs of Ptolemais, close to the dim plains of Helusion that border the foul Charonian canal.” Then all seven of us sprang from our seats in horror and stood trembling, shuddering and appalled. The tones of the shadow’s voice belonged not to one being but to a multitude. Changing their rhythm from syllable to syllable, they fell darkly on our ears in the familiar, well-remembered voices of many thousands of departed friends.
